topics.title: How do you test React components? Testing Library philosophy.
topics.html:
• Test behavior, not implementation. No assertions on internal state or component methods.
  • Query priority: getByRole → getByLabelText → getByPlaceholderText → getByText → getByTestId (last resort).
  • userEvent over fireEvent — simulates realistic input with delays.
test("shows error on invalid credentials", async () => {
  server.use(http.post("/api/login", () => HttpResponse.json({ message: "Invalid credentials" }, { status: 401 })));
  render(<LoginForm />);
  await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText("Email"), "bad@test.com");
  await userEvent.type(screen.getByLabelText("Password"), "wrong");
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /sign in/i }));
  expect(await screen.findByRole("alert")).toHaveTextContent("Invalid credentials");
});
💬 Say it like this

The core principle: test what the user sees and does, not how the component is implemented. If I refactor the internals but the behavior stays the same, my tests should still pass. I prefer getByRole for queries because it also validates accessibility — if a button has no accessible label, the query fails. For mocking network requests I use MSW — it intercepts at the network layer, so the same handlers work in unit tests, Storybook, and E2E tests.

Test pyramid vs test trophy?
Pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, few E2E. Trophy (Kent C. Dodds): integration tests are the base, fewer units (only complex logic), few E2E for critical paths. I lean trophy for frontend.
How do you fight flaky tests?
Replace sleeps with waitForSelector/waitForResponse. Use strict locators. Reset state via API between tests. Treat retries as a code smell, not a fix.

topics.title: Playwright & Page Object Model
topics.html:
class LoginPage {
  constructor(private page: Page) {}
  async login(email: string, password: string) {
    await this.page.getByLabel("Email").fill(email);
    await this.page.getByLabel("Password").fill(password);
    await this.page.getByRole("button", { name: /sign in/i }).click();
    await this.page.waitForURL("/dashboard");
  }
}
// Reuse auth state across tests — login once
export default defineConfig({ use: { storageState: "playwright/.auth/user.json" }, globalSetup: "./global-setup.ts" });
💬 Say it like this

The page object keeps the selectors and the actions of one screen in one class, so a change in the markup is fixed in one place instead of in twenty tests.

The other thing I always set up is logging in once and reusing the storage state, because logging in through the UI in every test is the slowest and the most flaky part of an end-to-end suite.

topics.title: Async UI tests — how do you wait for behavior without flaky sleeps?
topics.html:
Wait for a meaningful visible condition instead of guessing how many milliseconds the application needs. The query method expresses whether the element should already exist.

  • getByRole is for an element expected now; it throws if the expectation is not met.
  • findByRole waits for an element to appear. queryByRole supports an absence assertion without throwing.
  • Await userEvent interactions. A realistic interaction is a sequence, not just one synthetic event.
  • Use waitFor for an assertion that must eventually succeed. Its callback may run repeatedly, so do not click, submit, or mutate state inside it.

Control the network boundary with a deterministic test server or request mock, then assert what the user sees. Cover a rejected response and a delayed response as well as the successful path. Fake timers need deliberate integration with the interaction library; switching them on is not a universal speed improvement.

import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';

test('shows a saved confirmation', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  // The test fixture supplies a successful request response.
  render(<ProfileForm />);

  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Display name'), 'Alex');
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }));

  expect(await screen.findByRole('status')).toHaveTextContent('Saved');
  expect(screen.queryByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument();
});
In plain words

I wait for the UI outcome the user depends on, not for an arbitrary delay. Interactions happen outside retrying assertions, and each test controls its own network state so another test cannot decide its result.

Is waitFor(() => clickSave()) safe?
No. The callback can be retried, potentially submitting multiple requests. Perform the interaction once, then wait for an assertion about its outcome.
Can a role query replace every test ID?
Use semantic queries when they express a real user-facing contract. A test ID can be appropriate for a non-semantic integration boundary; adding fake roles purely to satisfy a test makes the UI less accurate.
